prompt: Which of these does the lesson give to the tech lead rather than the engineering manager?
hint: One answers for how the software is built.

choices.text: The commitments the team makes to the rest of the company
choices.why: Commitments to the company belong to the manager, who answers for what the team delivers.

choices.text: Whether people are still on the team a year from now
choices.why: Retention is in the manager’s half of the figure.

choices.text: Growth and feedback
choices.why: Growth and feedback are the manager’s; the tech lead gives technical feedback in review, which is a different thing.

choices.text: The quality bar in review
choices.why: Right: the review bar is part of how the software is built, the tech lead’s half.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a tech lead’s credibility depends on still writing code?
hint: What is a technical decision from somebody outside the codebase?

choices.text: Because the team measures leads by commits
choices.why: The lesson rejects commits as a measure of leadership in lesson 1; the point is informed judgement.

choices.text: Because a tech lead has no other way to contribute to the team
choices.why: Reviews, design and unblocking are contributions too, and they take a third of Diego’s week.

choices.text: Because company policy requires it of the role
choices.why: No policy is involved; the argument is about where technical judgement comes from.

choices.text: Without it, a design call is a guess with authority
choices.why: Right: the lesson’s phrase is “a guess with authority”, and staying in the code is what keeps the decisions informed.

prompt: Will Larson lists the tech lead as one of four shapes of which job?
hint: Look at the title of his book.

choices.text: A first-time manager’s, before they take on people
choices.why: The lesson draws the opposite conclusion: leading technically is a senior engineering job, not a junior management one.

choices.text: A product manager’s
choices.why: Product management is a different job and not one of Larson’s four.

choices.text: A director of engineering’s, who leads several managers at once
choices.why: Larson’s four shapes describe senior engineers who do not manage people.

choices.text: A senior engineer’s
choices.why: Right: tech lead sits beside architect, solver and right hand as a senior engineering role.

prompt: Match each item from the middle of the figure with the reason both leads touch it.
hint: Each side knows something the other does not.

pairs.right: one knows what the work involves, the other what the company needs and when
one judges technical skill, the other owns the hiring decision
one leads the response during it, the other schedules the follow-up after it
one knows who could do it, the other who needs it to grow

right_distractors: one writes the code, the other writes the tests

prompt: Diego said he wanted the manager’s job. What did the listening-tour conversation reveal?
hint: Which half of the figure did he want?

choices.text: He wanted the technical half, not the people half
choices.why: Right: he wanted the left half and assumed it came with the right, and nobody had offered it alone.

choices.text: He wanted the title and the pay that come with management
choices.why: Nothing in the conversation points to title or pay; it was about decisions over the software.

choices.text: He wanted to manage people and lacked experience
choices.why: When they listed what managing contained, he did not want most of it.

choices.text: He wanted to leave the team and was looking for a reason
choices.why: He stayed and took the tech lead role, which was what he had been after.

prompt: What is the mistake the lesson calls the worst in this area?
hint: Why do people take the management job?

choices.text: Going back to engineering after a few years of managing, which looks like failure to the team
choices.why: The lesson, following Charity Majors, calls that a normal career, not a failure.

choices.text: Taking management as the only way up, then being bad at it
choices.why: Right: the promotion framing pushes people into a job they never wanted.

choices.text: A manager reviewing pull requests
choices.why: Reviews are in the table of code that fits a manager’s week.

choices.text: A tech lead deciding by persuasion rather than authority
choices.why: The lesson calls that a feature as much as a cost.

prompt: A year into managing full-time, what does the lesson say usually still works, and what does not?
hint: Two kinds of technical knowledge decay at different speeds.

choices.text: Both are lost in the same year
choices.why: The lesson separates them precisely because they decay at different speeds.

choices.text: Currency with tools survives, but design judgement fades without daily practice
choices.why: It is the other way round: the specific, current knowledge is what goes first.

choices.text: Neither, if the manager keeps reading about technology
choices.why: Reading does not replace working in the codebase, which is where the specific knowledge comes from.

choices.text: Judgement, but not currency
choices.why: Right: knowing how a system should be designed lasts; knowing the framework version and the deploy tooling fades.

prompt: Which kinds of code fit a manager’s week, by the lesson’s table? Choose all that apply.
hint: Nobody should be waiting on it.

choices.text: Reviewing pull requests
choices.why: Yes: it keeps them current and fits between meetings.

choices.text: The most technically difficult ticket, to keep sharp
choices.why: No: difficulty is not the test; whether the plan depends on it is.

choices.text: Small fixes and tooling off the critical path
choices.why: Yes: nobody waits on them if a meeting runs over.

choices.text: Prototypes that will be thrown away
choices.why: Yes: they answer a question without becoming something to maintain.

choices.text: A feature with a date in the sprint plan
choices.why: No: that is the one kind the lesson rules out, because the team will wait for it.

prompt: Why does the lesson call a tech lead’s lack of formal authority a feature as much as a cost?

choices.text: Engineers argue more openly with somebody who does not decide their pay or promotion
choices.why: Right: without the review in their hands, disagreements about design happen in the open.

choices.text: It frees the tech lead from reviewing other people’s code
choices.why: Reviews are a large part of the tech lead’s week, a third of Diego’s.

choices.text: It means the tech lead never has to persuade anybody
choices.why: The opposite: without authority, persuasion is the main tool.

choices.text: Decisions get made faster, because nobody on the team is in a position to overrule a tech lead
choices.why: Speed is not the argument, and somebody can still overrule a design through the escalation the team agreed.

prompt: An engineer has managed for ten years and wants to go back to engineering. What does the lesson’s reasoning predict?

choices.text: An easy move, because judgement does not decay
choices.why: Judgement holds up, but the specific knowledge the job needs daily has gone.

choices.text: A failure, which the pendulum essay warns against
choices.why: The essay argues the opposite: moving back is a normal career.

choices.text: A move the company should refuse, since the dual track does not allow it
choices.why: A dual track exists to make such moves possible; nothing in the lesson says it forbids them.

choices.text: A restart, not a return
choices.why: Right: the lesson puts two or three years away as a return and ten as a restart.

prompt: Charity Majors’s 2017 essay compares the move between engineering and management to a ___.
Why does every row of the agreement have exactly one name under “decides”?
hint: What is a decision with two deciders?

choices.text: So that the manager can always overrule the tech lead
choices.why: Several rows give the decision to Diego, so it does not put Renata on top.

choices.text: Because HR requires a single owner for each decision
choices.why: Nobody outside the two asked for the page; the reason is the conflict in the team channel.

choices.text: A decision with two deciders is a decision with none
choices.why: Right: two owners means both act, and they disagree in front of the team, as with Thiago.

choices.text: To keep the page short enough that the team will read it
choices.why: Length is not the reason; a page with two deciders per row would be no longer.

prompt: Renata and Diego disagree about the design of a feature, which the page gives to Diego. What does their second rule say happens?
hint: Argue where, then who decides, then what in public?

choices.text: They argue in private, Diego decides, and Renata supports it in public
choices.why: Right: the owner decides after a private argument, and the other backs the decision in front of the team.

choices.text: Renata decides, because she is Diego’s manager
choices.why: The page gives design to Diego, and being his manager does not move that row.

choices.text: They take it to the team and vote
choices.why: The rule keeps the disagreement private; a vote would put it in front of the team.

choices.text: They escalate it to Otávio, who decides between them
choices.why: Otávio is informed about some rows; he does not arbitrate the ones already assigned.

prompt: Why does the lesson say the page matters more than the conversation that produced it?
hint: How do people remember an agreement?

choices.text: Because a written agreement is legally binding
choices.why: Nothing about this is legal; it is about what people can point at.

choices.text: Because the conversation happened before the split
choices.why: It happened after the split, the week of the calendar-sync messages.

choices.text: Memory drifts, and the team reads a page
choices.why: Right: two reasons in the lesson, the drift of memory and the team being able to read the page.

choices.text: Because conversations between leads are never honest
choices.why: The lesson does not doubt the conversation’s honesty, only how it is remembered later.

prompt: A team has a tech lead and a manager. In planning, the tech lead says a feature takes six weeks and the manager has already told the director four. Which row of an agreement like Agenda’s was missing?
hint: Which item from the middle of the figure is this?

choices.text: Who decides the team’s commitments, and who is consulted first
choices.why: Right: on Agenda, Renata decides commitments after consulting Diego, which would have caught the gap before the director heard a number.

choices.text: Who decides how the feature is designed
choices.why: The disagreement is about the date promised, not the design.

choices.text: Who leads the technical response during an incident
choices.why: There is no incident here.

choices.text: Whether a pull request meets the bar
choices.why: Review standards have nothing to do with the estimate given upwards.

prompt: Put the steps of the agreement’s second rule in order, for a disagreement about a decision that already has an owner.
items: Both argue their case in private
The owner of the decision decides
The other supports the decision in public
trap: Supporting in public before the private argument has happened means the disagreement is never heard.
